0.title: The Sound Church: Titus and the Gospel-Ordered Life
0.overview:
The message. Titus is the shortest of Paul’s three letters to pastors: three tightly packed chapters that move from doctrine to character to conduct without pausing. Its burden is that true belief and a godly life belong together: the truth “accords with godliness” (1:1), so a church that holds it must look like it, in its leaders, its homes and its dealings with outsiders. Beneath the instructions lies the gospel: the grace of God that saves us also trains us, and Christ “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (2:14).

Background: the writer and his delegate. The letter names Paul as its author (1:1). He had left Titus on Crete with a large assignment: “put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town” (1:5). Titus is never named in Acts, but Paul’s other letters show him: a Greek convert whom Paul took to Jerusalem uncircumcised (Galatians 2:1–3), a living test case of the gospel of grace. Later he was Paul’s trusted envoy to troubled Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:6–15; 8:16–23). Paul calls him “my true child in a common faith” (1:4). He was not a bishop of Crete in the later sense, but Paul’s delegate for a season; Artemas or Tychicus would replace him, and he was to join Paul for the winter at Nicopolis, probably the city on the west coast of Greece (3:12).

When and from where. Paul’s only recorded visit to Crete was as a prisoner, when his ship sheltered at Fair Havens on the way to Rome (Acts 27:7–13). The mission the letter assumes must therefore come later. Most likely Paul was released from the house arrest with which Acts closes (Acts 28:30–31), worked on Crete with Titus, and moved on. He probably wrote about AD 62–64, perhaps from Macedonia, around the time of 1 Timothy and before his final imprisonment. Zenas the lawyer and Apollos may have carried it (3:13).

Crete and the Cretans. Crete, the long, mountainous island at the southern edge of the Aegean, was famous in antiquity: Homer called it the island of a hundred cities, and it had been home to the palace of Knossos and the Minoan civilisation. In Paul’s day it formed a Roman province with Cyrenaica in North Africa. It had a Jewish community, and Cretans heard Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:11). It also had a reputation for dishonesty so notorious that the Greeks coined a verb, “to Cretanise”, meaning to lie. Paul quotes a line traditionally ascribed to Epimenides, a Cretan seer of about the sixth century BC: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons” (1:12). This is no racial insult: a Cretan said it, and the false teachers have proved it true (1:13). Against them the letter sets the “God, who never lies” (1:2).

What prompted the letter. The churches were young, still without settled leaders, and under pressure from teachers Paul calls “insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party” (1:10). They were devoted to “Jewish myths and the commands of people” (1:14), to “foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law” (3:9). Paul’s reply, “To the pure, all things are pure” (1:15), suggests they also laid down purity rules. They were “upsetting whole families” for “shameful gain” (1:11), and “They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works” (1:16). The error resembles the one Timothy faced at Ephesus.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think a later follower wrote the three Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy and Titus) in Paul’s name, pointing to their vocabulary and style, their concern for church order, and travels that do not fit into Acts. But the letter names Paul, the early church received it as his, and the church order it describes is simple: a plurality of elders, also called overseers (1:5, 7), such as Paul appointed from his first journey (Acts 14:23). Differences of style suit an older apostle writing to a trusted co-worker on new subjects, and the travels fit a release after Acts. A letter falsely claiming to be Paul’s would be a forgery, which the early church rejected. The more likely conclusion, and the view of this commentary, is that Paul wrote it.

How the letter makes its case. Its key word is “sound” (hygiainō: healthy, health-giving): sound doctrine (1:9; 2:1), sound in the faith (1:13; 2:2), sound speech (2:8). False teaching makes people sick; sound doctrine makes healthy churches. Chapter 1 grounds everything in God’s eternal promise of life (1:1–4), then sets out the elders Crete needs, men of proven character who can “give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it” (1:5–9), and exposes the false teachers they must answer (1:10–16). Chapter 2 tells Titus what to teach each group (2:1–10): older men, older women who train the younger, younger women, younger men, Titus himself as their model, and slaves, each with a reason that looks outward, so that slaves “may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (2:10). Then comes the foundation: grace has appeared, “training us to renounce ungodliness” while we wait for Christ’s appearing (2:11–15). Chapter 3 turns to life among unbelieving neighbours, submissive and courteous (3:1–2), because “we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray” until God saved us by his mercy (3:3–7). Titus is to insist on this “so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works” (3:8), to avoid pointless quarrels and deal firmly with a divisive person (3:9–11); news and greetings close the letter (3:12–15).

Where it leads: to Christ. The letter calls God “our Savior” three times (1:3; 2:10; 3:4), and each time follows soon with Christ as Saviour (1:4; 2:13; 3:6), so that the saving work of the Father and the Son is one. It stands between two appearings. The grace of God “has appeared, bringing salvation for all people” (2:11) in Christ’s first coming; believers now wait for “the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (2:13), one of the New Testament’s plainest statements that Jesus is God. And 3:4–7 is one of the richest summaries of salvation in Paul’s letters: God saved us “not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit”, so that “being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life”. This commentary takes the washing to be the Spirit’s cleansing new birth, of which baptism is the sign. The letter that sounds like a manual of church order is, at its root, a letter about grace.

For us. Titus refuses to let doctrine and life drift apart. It tells churches to choose leaders for their character and their grip on the truth, and to expect sound teaching to produce changed homes and honest work. It shows that ordinary faithfulness, a self-controlled older man, a kind young mother, an honest worker, can make the gospel attractive to people who will never read a theology book. And it keeps us humble and gentle toward outsiders by reminding us what we once were. We do good works not to be saved, but because the grace that saved us is training us to be a people eager to do good.

1.title: The Ordered Church: Elders, Sound Doctrine, and False Teachers
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the letter. After a greeting rooted in God’s eternal promise, Paul turns straight to the work he left Titus on Crete to do, appointing elders, and to why it cannot wait: false teachers are already at work.

The message. The truth God has spoken, promised by a God who never lies, produces godly lives. So the churches need leaders whose homes, characters and teaching match that truth, and must refuse teachers whose lives deny it. Knowing God shows in what a person is and does, not only in what he says.

Why it was said. The young churches on Crete had no settled leaders, and teachers, many from the circumcision party, were peddling myths and purity rules and overturning whole households for money (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First the foundation (vv. 1–4): Paul serves the faith of God’s elect and a knowledge of the truth that “accords with godliness”, resting on the hope promised by the God who never lies, and he greets Titus, a Gentile, as his true son in a common faith. Then the remedy (vv. 5–9): elders in every town, above reproach at home, stewards of God’s household free of self-will and greed, holding the word firmly enough to feed the flock and refute opponents. They are described with the danger in view. Then the danger (vv. 10–16): empty talkers to be silenced and sharply rebuked so that people become sound (vv. 10–13), whose purity rules miss that defilement lives in the mind and conscience (vv. 14–15), and who profess to know God but deny him by their works (v. 16). The chapter ends on the test it began with.

Where it leads. The God who never lies kept his oldest promise in his Son, the eternal life that was with the Father (1 John 1:2). The elder is only a steward in Christ’s house, and the list of his qualities describes one man without a flaw; the pure are those Christ has washed; the cure for an island of liars is faith in the one who is the truth. The grace that reached Crete did not wait for a better people.

For us. Ask whether what you believe shows in your home, your money and your tongue. Choose leaders for their character, not their polish. And rest your weight on a word that has never once been broken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything Titus is about to do rests on a promise older than the world, made by a God who never lies. Paul presents himself as God’s servant and Christ’s apostle, sent to bring God’s chosen people to a faith and a knowledge of the truth that show in godly lives (v. 1). That faith rests on the hope of eternal life, promised before the ages began and now made known in the preaching entrusted to him (vv. 2–3). Then he greets Titus, a Greek believer, as his true son in a faith they share on equal terms (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Cannot Lie, Writing to Crete

The first thing Paul says about God, to an island famous for lying, is that he never lies; and his eternal promise reaches people only through preaching (see the note on vv. 1–3).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Titus was the uncircumcised test case at Jerusalem and the man sent into the Corinthian crisis (see “The setting” at vv. 1–3 and the note on v. 4).

Now: Knowledge of the truth is recognised by the godliness it produces (v. 1).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s whole ministry serves God’s eternal promise of life, made by a God who never lies and now made known through the preaching entrusted to him. He works to bring God’s chosen people to faith and to a knowledge of the truth that shows itself in a godly life.

An unusually long opening. For so short a letter the opening sentence is remarkably long, and the length is the point: before a word of instruction, Paul sets out where the truth comes from.

Paul, a servant of God. Servant here means slave. Only here does Paul call himself a servant of God (elsewhere, of Christ Jesus), a title that places him with Moses, David and the prophets (Joshua 1:2; Jeremiah 7:25). It is the lowest word in the Roman household and the highest title in Israel’s Scriptures, and Paul wears both meanings at once.

And an apostle of Jesus Christ. Servant expresses humility; apostle, authority. The pairing appears nowhere else in Paul, and it sets God and Christ side by side (see the note on v. 4).

For the sake of the faith of God’s elect. Paul’s apostleship exists to bring God’s chosen ones to faith and to build it up. God chose a people; Paul preaches so that they will believe (2 Timothy 2:10; Acts 13:48). That is why a missionary can land on an island of liars and expect a church (see the box below).

Which accords with godliness. Full knowledge, knowing that has taken hold, and it leads to godliness. Truth is recognised by the life it produces; a knowledge that leaves a man unchanged is not what Paul means, however much he knows (v. 16).

What godliness is. The word sounds old-fashioned, even stiff and joyless. In Paul’s letters it means a life turned towards God, lived in reverence and trust with him in view; its opposite need not be wild, but is simply living as if God were not there (2:12). So godliness is first a relationship, which is why Paul ties it to knowing the truth: you cannot be centred on a God you do not know. We see it whole in Christ, who said, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and through him we come to God as children. In ordinary life it shows in small things: thanks before a meal, a decision prayed over before it is made rather than after, a Lord’s Day kept for him, and the quiet habit of asking, “What would please him here?”

In hope of eternal life. Hope is confident expectation, and faith, knowledge and godliness all rest on it (3:7). The Christian is not godly in order to earn a future; he is godly because a future has been promised to him and is certain.

Which God, who never lies, promised. “Who never lies” is one Greek word, “unlying”, found only here in the New Testament. Writing to an island whose own poet said “Cretans are always liars” (v. 12), the first thing Paul says about God is that he cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Hebrews 6:18). The promise was made “before the ages began” (as in 2 Timothy 1:9), within the Trinity, in what is sometimes called the covenant of redemption: before anything was made, the Father gave a people to the Son, and the Son undertook to come and lay down his life for them (John 6:37–39; 17:2, 6).

Manifested in his word through the preaching. “At the proper time” means in his own seasons (1 Timothy 2:6): what God promised in eternity, he made visible in history through the preached gospel.

By the command of God our Saviour. “Entrusted” means put into Paul’s care (1 Timothy 1:11). That is how an eternal promise reaches anybody: through people trusted to preach it, so appointing the right men in every town (v. 5) is not mere administration. God our Saviour is one of six Saviour titles in this short letter: three times the Father (1:3; 2:10; 3:4), and three times Christ (1:4; 2:13; 3:6), once as our great God and Saviour.

The life that was with the Father. What was promised and then brought into the open? John answers: “the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us” (1 John 1:2). The life promised to the elect is Christ himself (1 John 5:12), so the manifesting at the proper time was not only a sermon but a birth, a cross and an empty tomb, which the preaching announces.

A word never broken. On an island where a man’s word was worth little, the God who cannot lie had kept his word for longer than there had been islands. He gave it before the ages began, held to it through the fall, the flood, the exile and four silent centuries, and kept it at last at the cost of his own Son’s life. Every one of his chosen, on Crete or anywhere, stands on a word that has never once been broken.

In everyday life. Most lies are small and social: the excuse for being late, the story improved in the telling, the flattering answer. They seem harmless, but they are the Cretan habit in modern dress. A person who belongs to the God who never lies is free to be plainly truthful, and to let a yes be yes.

If God has chosen his elect, why should I share the gospel? Because God has chosen to save his elect through the gospel being shared. Election decides who will be saved; preaching is how they are reached (2 Timothy 2:10). You do not know who the elect are, and you do not need to. Speak to everyone, pray for everyone, and trust God to open the hearts he has chosen to open, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14). Election is evangelism’s great encouragement: your words are not wasted, because God has a people and he will call them.

How can I know if I am one of God’s elect? Not by looking into God’s secret decrees, but by looking to Christ. Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37), and no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). If you trust Christ, love him and want to follow him, that is the evidence that God chose you. If you are unsure, do not wait to discover whether you are chosen; come to Christ now. Election is a doctrine for believers to rejoice in, not a barrier for seekers.

Isn’t every claim to truth a bid for power? Michel Foucault taught many to ask of any claim to truth not “Is it true?” but “Who gains if I believe it?” The question is not foolish; Paul is about to expose teachers who peddle religion for shameful gain (v. 11). But turned on everything, it saws off the branch it sits on, since “all truth is power” is itself offered as true. And the truth of this passage does not come from the strong to keep the weak in line. It was promised by a God who owed no one a promise, and brought into the open in a man who had all power and laid it down, was falsely accused, and died for those who lied about him. Timothy Keller often pointed out that a faith whose central figure dies for his enemies, praying for their forgiveness, carries within it the means to judge every abuse of power done in its name. In a world worn out by spin, the God who never lies is not a threat but a relief.

Where Christians differ: does election come before faith, or rest on it? Arminian Christians (named after the Dutch teacher Jacob Arminius) hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe; they love and preach the gospel. This commentary’s view: the hope was promised before the ages began (v. 2), and God saved us because of “his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began” (2 Timothy 1:9). The more likely reading is that election comes first and faith is its fruit.
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek convert and one of Paul’s trusted troubleshooters. The letter was probably written between Paul’s two Roman imprisonments, in the mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.quote: To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Titus is Paul’s genuine son in the faith, sharing it with him on equal terms, and Paul greets him with grace and peace from the Father and from Christ, both named as Saviour.

To Titus, my true child. “True” means genuine, the same word used of Timothy (1 Timothy 1:2). Titus was probably converted through Paul and is his authorised representative, the man Paul sent into hard places: first troubled Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:6–7), now Crete.

In a common faith. Common means shared, not ordinary. Paul the Jew and Titus the Gentile hold one faith, which mattered in a church troubled by the circumcision party (v. 10). There is no second-class place in it: every believer has the same Saviour, who gave himself for all of them alike.

Grace and peace. Christ is called Saviour just after the Father is (v. 3). The switch is not careless: it places Christ with God, as Paul will say outright at 2:13, “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ”.

What does it mean to be someone’s child in the faith? It is the bond with the person God used to bring you to Christ or nurture you early on: a real family tie, with love, gratitude and responsibility on both sides, though not ownership; Titus is sent off to lead on his own. A parent, a Sunday school teacher, a friend who explained the gospel, a pastor who walked with you: thank God for them, and ask him to let you be that for someone else.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add “mercy”, reading “grace, mercy and peace”, as in 1 and 2 Timothy. The earlier manuscripts have only “grace and peace”, very probably what Paul wrote; the addition looks like a copyist bringing Titus into line with the letters to Timothy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Appointing Elders in Every Town
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The disorder on Crete is to be met by the right leaders: men of proven character who hold God’s word firmly. Titus is to appoint elders in every town (v. 5), men above reproach in marriage and home (v. 6), stewards of God’s household who are free of self-will, temper, drink, violence and greed, and are welcoming, good, self-controlled and devout (vv. 7–8). Their one required skill grows out of that character: holding the apostles’ teaching so as to feed the flock with sound doctrine and refute those who oppose it (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Elder and Overseer Are One Office

‘Elders’ (v. 5) and ‘overseer’ (v. 7) name one office within a single sentence; and of the qualifications, eleven concern character and only one concerns ability: to teach and to rebuke (v. 9; see the note on vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations existed across Crete without yet being in working order (v. 5).

Now: On ‘children are believers’ (v. 6), see the box “Where Christians differ: must an elder’s children be converted?” at the end of the note on vv. 5–6.

verseByVerse.quote: This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Titus is to finish setting the young churches in order by appointing elders in every town, men whose marriages and homes show a life no one can fairly accuse.

This is why I left you in Crete. Not abandoned: the verb describes a deliberate posting, after Paul’s release from his first imprisonment (see the introduction).

So that you might put what remained into order. “What remained” admits the work was unfinished: the churches were real but not yet in working order, and the chief need was proper leadership.

And appoint elders in every town. “Elders” is plural: each town’s church was to have several (Acts 14:23). Paul’s answer to disorder is not one strong man at the centre but properly appointed leaders in each place, so Titus seems meant to work himself out of a job. Churches differ over how this pattern is carried on, but all agree that every church needs qualified, godly leaders.

As I directed you. Instructions already given in person are now in writing, so that nobody on Crete could say Titus was acting on his own.

In the flow. The whole letter turns on verse 5. The right men must be put in place (vv. 6–9) because the wrong men are already talking (vv. 10–16); then households (chapter 2) and citizens (chapter 3) can be taught to live in a way that fits sound doctrine.

If anyone is above reproach. Nothing in his life that anyone can fairly bring against him (compare 1 Timothy 3:10). It is the headline qualification, repeated in verse 7, and the list runs closely parallel to 1 Timothy 3.

The husband of one wife. Literally a one-woman man: faithful in marriage (1 Timothy 3:2). Some read it as forbidding polygamy, remarriage or singleness; the more likely reading is that Paul asks for a man faithful to his wife. A single man is not excluded, since Paul himself was single. A man divorced long ago, or as the innocent party, may qualify if his life is now above reproach, and the church must judge each case with care. The qualification also assumes that elders are men, as in 1 Timothy 2:12 and 3:2. This commentary holds that the office of elder belongs to qualified men (a view often called complementarian), because Paul grounds it in creation rather than local custom (1 Timothy 2:13). Many faithful Christians read these passages differently, and the point is never that women are less gifted or less valued: Paul’s letters are full of women in gospel work (Romans 16:1–7).

And his children are believers. Children still at home, under his authority, who are not wild or rebellious; in 1 Timothy an overseer must keep his children submissive (1 Timothy 3:4). On the word itself, see the boxes below.

Debauchery or insubordination. Debauchery is wild, reckless living, the word family used of the prodigal son (Luke 15:13); insubordination is rebellion. If an elder cannot lead his own household, he cannot lead the church (1 Timothy 3:5).

Why does Paul care so much about an elder’s home? Because the home is where a man’s character is seen without a pulpit. Anyone can look godly for an hour on Sunday; his wife and children see him on Monday night. A man harsh, absent or indifferent at home will be the same with the church, and one who leads his family with patient, self-giving love is showing the very skills a church needs. For every Christian husband and father, elder or not, the home is the first congregation.

A flock bought with blood. Why does it matter so much who leads a house church in a Cretan town? Because the church is the flock God obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28), and its elders are under-shepherds answering to the Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4). A man who will not give himself for his own wife and children cannot be trusted with people for whom Christ gave himself. The husband of one wife is to love her as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25), so that his marriage becomes a small copy of the true Shepherd’s faithfulness.

In everyday life. An elder’s wife and children carry the weight of the church as well as their own, and are rarely thanked. A meal left on the step, an evening of babysitting or a kind note can be the quiet support that keeps a shepherd’s household strong.

If my child has walked away from the faith, have I failed? Not necessarily, and do not carry a guilt God has not laid on you. No parent can give a child a new heart (John 1:13). Faithful parents in Scripture had wayward children, and God himself, the perfect Father, had rebellious children in Israel (Isaiah 1:2). Ask honestly whether there are ways you need to repent, and confess them to God and, where it would help, to your child. Then keep praying, keep loving, keep the door open and keep living the gospel in front of them. The prodigal’s father never stopped watching the road.

Where Christians differ: must an elder’s children be converted? Some insist that all an elder’s children must be professing Christians. This commentary’s view: since conversion is God’s work and not under a father’s control (John 1:13), and the word can mean faithful in the sense of trustworthy, it is better to read this as requiring that his children at home be orderly and respectful, not openly wild or rebellious. A father who has faithfully raised his children and whose child has not yet professed faith is not thereby disqualified, but a household in open disorder would disqualify him.

Uncertain wording. The Greek word translated “believers” (pista) can mean believing or faithful (trustworthy), and both senses are common. The phrase that follows, “not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination”, and the parallel in 1 Timothy 3:4 suggest the likely meaning: children who are faithful and well ordered, with their conduct rather than their profession in view.
verseByVerse.note: Crete is a large island south of Greece. Acts records Paul only touching at it as a prisoner (Acts 27:7–13); this later work there is not in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: For an overseer, as God's steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because an elder manages God’s household, not his own, he must be a man of tested character who holds the apostles’ teaching firmly enough to feed the church and to answer those who oppose it.

For an overseer. Elder in verse 5, overseer (episkopos) here: two words, in one sentence, for one set of men. Elders and overseers (bishops) were the same people, as scholars of most traditions agree.

As God’s steward, must be above reproach. The steward is the household manager. The title carries real authority and no ownership whatever: he spends another man’s money and answers for it (1 Timothy 3:15).

He must not be arrogant. Then five things he must not be. “Arrogant” means self-willed, the man who suits himself. Underneath is usually a hunger for control, the fear of what might happen if he were not in charge. Only a man who no longer needs to run everything, because he trusts the one who does, can be trusted with a church.

Or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent. The man with a short fuse; the drinker; the striker, who hits people with his fists or his words (1 Timothy 3:3).

Or greedy for gain. Fond of dishonest profit (1 Timothy 3:8). On Crete this was the live issue: the false teachers were in it for shameful gain (v. 11), and a man who wants money should not be given charge of a church’s.

But hospitable, a lover of good. Then six things he must be. “Hospitable” is literally a lover of strangers; a “lover of good” is the opposite of those who in the last days will not love good (2 Timothy 3:3).

Self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. “Self-controlled” means sensible, of sound mind; “upright”, just in his dealings with people; “holy”, devout toward God; and “disciplined”, in control of his desires: a man with a grip on himself.

Character first. Every item so far is about character; only verse 9 gives the single competence. On an island of empty talkers (v. 10), a true elder was never going to be told apart from a false teacher by how well he could talk.

He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught. To cling to it against opposition: the apostles’ teaching as it was handed to him, not his own improved version.

Instruction in sound doctrine. “Sound” means healthy, the word from which we get hygiene: sound doctrine makes people spiritually well. This is his positive task, feeding the flock.

Rebuke those who contradict it. Refute, expose, convict those who speak against it. This is his negative task, protecting the flock from wolves. A man who can only encourage will watch the flock be eaten; a man who can only refute will do the eating himself. Paul requires both.

A steward in the Son’s house. The steward runs a house that is not his, and Hebrews names its owner: Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over it as a son, and we are his house (Hebrews 3:5–6). The elder is never master of the congregation, but a servant managing the Son’s household, spending what the Son bought and answering to him for every soul (Hebrews 13:17). A self-willed steward behaves as though the house were his; a greedy one helps himself to what belongs to another. Both have forgotten whose house it is.

Every quality, without a flaw. One man has borne every quality in this list without a flaw. He came not to do his own will; he was slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love; never violent or greedy, he gave himself and his blood for his church. He held the Father’s word so firmly that he answered the devil with it, and he will not lose one of his sheep.

What hospitality looks like. Required of elders, hospitality is commanded of every Christian (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), and it is simpler than we fear. It is not entertaining; nobody needs a tidy house or an impressive meal. Invite someone who would not otherwise be invited: the newcomer at church, the student far from home, the widower, the family down the road. Keep it ordinary: soup and bread, or one more place at a table you were already laying. Ask questions and listen. Open the door more than once, because friendship grows by repetition; if your home cannot hold guests, take the welcome to theirs, or meet in a café. Behind it stands the welcome we were given: strangers and enemies, brought in by Christ at the cost of his life, “no longer strangers and aliens” but members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:19; Romans 15:7). Every meal shared with a stranger is a small picture of that welcome and a foretaste of his feast. An open door and an extra plate were how the early church grew, and they still are.

How should a church choose its elders? By looking for these qualities over time, not by electing the most successful, wealthy or outspoken men. Watch how a man treats his family, handles money, takes criticism and serves when no one is looking. Ask whether he knows and loves the Bible, can explain it, and can gently but firmly answer error. Give him time to be tested (1 Timothy 3:10; 5:22), and pray before laying hands on anyone. Churches differ on who makes the final choice, the congregation, the elders or a wider body, but the qualities are the same, and they are the ones God wants in every believer; elders are simply men in whom they are mature enough to be an example.

What if my elders fall short of this list? Every elder falls short in some measure; pray for them and bear with their weaknesses as they bear with yours. A minor fault can be raised privately and kindly, or covered with love (1 Peter 4:8). A serious and persistent pattern of anger, drunkenness, greed, harshness or false teaching should be raised with the other elders, with evidence (1 Timothy 5:19–20). An elder clearly disqualified should step down, and a church does him no kindness by pretending otherwise. Never use the list as a weapon; use it as a standard everyone is glad to be held to.
verseByVerse.note: “Elder” (v. 5) and “overseer” here describe the same office.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teachers whose lives deny the God they claim to know must be stopped, for the sake of the households they are ruining. Many are talking, especially from the circumcision party, and they are overturning whole families for money (vv. 10–11). A Cretan proverb fits them, so Titus must rebuke them sharply, aiming at health (vv. 12–13). Their myths and man-made purity rules miss where defilement really lives, in the mind and conscience (vv. 14–15), and their works deny the God they profess (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Quoting a Pagan, and Agreeing With Him

Paul endorses Epimenides' verdict on Crete, though not as a racial claim (see the note on vv. 12–13), and he rebukes sharply so that the offenders ‘may be sound in the faith’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Deceivers overturning whole households must be silenced, while the deceived are handled gently (see the note on vv. 10–11).

Now: ‘To the pure all things are pure’ (v. 15) does away with ritual uncleanness, not sin (see the note on vv. 14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The right elders are urgently needed because many deceivers, especially from the circumcision party, are ruining whole households for money, and their mouths must be stopped.

For there are many who are insubordinate. “Many” is a sobering word: the troublemakers on Crete were not a small fringe. “Insubordinate” means refusing to be under anything, the word used of an elder’s children in verse 6.

Empty talkers and deceivers. Vain-speakers whose words carry nothing (1 Timothy 1:6), and mind-deceivers: there is nothing in what they say, and it still leads people astray.

Especially those of the circumcision party. Jewish Christians, or those influenced by them, who insisted on circumcision and the law of Moses, as in Galatia (Galatians 2:12; Acts 15:1, 5), mixing in Jewish myths, purity rules and speculation (v. 14; 3:9). Titus knew what was at stake: he had been the test case at Jerusalem (Galatians 2:3).

They must be silenced. To stop the mouth, as with a muzzle: not by force, but by refuting them with sound doctrine (v. 9) and refusing them a platform in the church. Gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25) is for the deceived; silencing is for the deceivers, because a congregation can be destroyed while the discussion goes on.

Upsetting whole families. “Upsetting” means overturning, as in 2 Timothy 2:18. Since churches met in homes, a household overturned could mean a whole house church lost at once.

Teaching for shameful gain. They taught for money (1 Timothy 6:5), the very thing that disqualifies an elder (v. 7).

Christ plus nothing. Why was the circumcision party so dangerous? Because to demand circumcision as a condition of belonging to God is to say that Christ is not enough; accept it on those terms, Paul told the Galatians, and Christ is of no advantage to you (Galatians 5:2–4). A teaching that adds a rite to the cross does not add to the gospel; it replaces it. Titus, the uncircumcised test case, could not treat it as a difference of emphasis while whole families were being taught to trust in something besides Christ.

The Good Shepherd does not fleece his sheep. He gave his life for them. The false teachers on Crete came for what they could get; Christ came with nothing to gain and everything to give, and one day every empty word will be silenced and his voice alone will be heard.

What it does not mean. Not that Jewish believers were the problem as such; Paul himself was Jewish. The problem was teaching that added the law to Christ. Nor does “silenced” mean persecution or civil punishment.

How does a church silence false teachers today? By Paul’s means, not by force. Elders who know the Bible answer the error clearly and publicly. False teachers are not given the pulpit, the Bible study, the youth group or the newsletter. A member who persists in spreading serious error after patient correction may have to be removed (3:10–11). Online, it means not sharing such teaching, and warning those in your care. None of this involves cruelty, slander or calling on the state. It is a shepherd closing the gate on the wolf.

Is it wrong for a teacher to be paid? No. Those who labour in preaching and teaching deserve support (1 Timothy 5:17–18). The sin is teaching for shameful gain: shaping the message to make money or to please the paying audience. The signs are not hard to spot: constant appeals for money, promises that giving will make you rich, a lifestyle far above the people who fund it, and no accountability. Support faithful teachers gladly; be wary of anyone whose message always ends with your wallet.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons." This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Cretan’s own proverb fits these teachers exactly, so Titus must rebuke them sharply, with the aim of making people healthy in the faith.

One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said. A pagan, usually identified as Epimenides of Knossos, a sixth-century BC Cretan poet the Greeks regarded as a seer. Paul calls him a prophet only because the Cretans did, not because God spoke through him; he quotes Greek poets in the same way elsewhere (Acts 17:28).

Cretans are always liars. The reputation was proverbial (see the introduction). One reason: Cretans claimed to have the tomb of Zeus, which other Greeks counted the great Cretan lie, since they believed Zeus could not die. The contrast with the God who never lies (v. 2) is pointed.

Evil beasts, lazy gluttons. Wild, dangerous animals; and literally idle bellies, people driven by their appetites and unwilling to work.

This testimony is true. Paul agrees flatly, but read him carefully. The proverb describes the false teachers well: they lie, they are brutal in upsetting families, and they are driven by greed. It is not a racial claim about Cretans as such: Paul has just left elders and congregations there for Titus to build up. A Cretan said this about Crete; Paul agrees that it fits these men.

Therefore rebuke them sharply. “Sharply” means cuttingly; its root is the verb to cut off. Timothy was told to be gentle and patient (2 Timothy 2:25); Titus, on Crete, to cut. Paul has more than one tone of voice, and a minister with only one has not learned from him.

That they may be sound in the faith. The sharpness aims at health. “They” probably means the church members being influenced, and perhaps the false teachers themselves. A rebuke meant to make someone healthy is a different act from one meant to put him in his place, even when the words are identical.

Sound in the faith of the truthful one. What makes a liar healthy? The rebuke clears the way; the cure is the faith it calls people back to, and that faith rests on a person: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), who came not for the healthy but for the sick (Mark 2:17). The gospel came to an island of liars, beasts and idle bellies and planted churches in it. God does not wait for a better people. He sent his Son to the Cretans, and to us, and makes liars truthful, savages gentle, and the lazy zealous for good works.

What it does not mean. It does not license ethnic stereotyping of people today. Paul’s aim is that Cretans become sound in the faith.

In everyday life. The grace that reached Crete does not leave a people as it finds them. Name one sin your culture or family is known for, one you are tempted to excuse because everyone shares it, and ask God this week to make you different there.

Is the saying self-refuting, since a Cretan said all Cretans are liars? Logicians have enjoyed the puzzle, but it is not what Paul is doing. It is a proverb about a people’s character, not a claim about every Cretan on every occasion. And quoting a pagan writer’s true statement no more makes him an inspired prophet than quoting a newspaper makes it Scripture. All truth is God’s truth, and Paul uses it wherever he finds it.

How do I know when to rebuke sharply and when gently? Look at the person and the danger. Gentleness is right for the confused, the weak, the stumbling young believer, and anyone willing to listen (Galatians 6:1; 2 Timothy 2:24–25). Sharpness is right when someone is knowingly leading others astray, when gentle words have been ignored, or when great harm must be stopped at once. Even then, aim at the person’s health, never your own satisfaction: would you be glad if they repented and you never got the credit? Most of us lean to one tone; ask God for the other when it is needed.
verseByVerse.note: The line is usually traced to Epimenides, a Cretan poet-prophet of about 600 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Purity is a matter of the heart, not of rules about food and washing: to the cleansed, God’s created gifts are clean, but a defiled mind and conscience stain everything they touch. So the teachers’ myths and man-made rules cannot make anyone pure.

Not devoting themselves to Jewish myths. Speculative stories and legends drawn from Jewish tradition, not Scripture itself: the same material as at Ephesus, myths and endless genealogies (1 Timothy 1:4).

And the commands of people. Human rules, which Jesus condemned (Mark 7:7–8, quoting Isaiah 29:13), probably purity rules about food and washing (v. 15). Myths and man-made rules look like opposites, yet they regularly arrive together, because both offer what grace does not: secret knowledge to feel superior with, and rules to keep and measure yourself by. Each lets a religious man feel he stands before God on his own achievement, and the gospel takes that away from both.

To the pure, all things are pure. A genuine principle: purity is a matter of the heart, not of external rules. Against teachers imposing food laws and ritual restrictions, Paul says that for those whose hearts have been cleansed by faith (Acts 15:9), no food or created thing is defiling in itself (Mark 7:15; 1 Timothy 4:4).

But to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. The uncleanness is in the person, not the thing. A corrupted mind corrupts whatever it handles, even good and innocent things, and rules about food cannot clean it, because the trouble is not in the food.

Both their minds and their consciences are defiled. The mind judges what is true; the conscience, what is right. When both are stained, nothing is left inside that can detect the problem (1 Timothy 4:2), which is why such men are confident, and why they must be silenced rather than reasoned with.

Who makes the pure pure. By nature every mind and conscience is defiled, so where do pure people come from? From Christ, twice over. He declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), setting aside the very rules the Cretan teachers pressed; and his blood cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). The pure of verse 15 are not better rule-keepers but defiled people whom Christ has washed, and to them he hands back the created world as clean.

The current ran the other way. Under the old law, touching the unclean made a man unclean. Then the Holy One came, and the current ran the other way. He laid his hand on a leper, and the leper was clean; a woman who had bled for twelve years touched his garment and was made well. Nothing defiled could defile him, and whatever he touched in mercy he made pure. At the last he went outside the camp and bore our uncleanness himself.

What it does not mean. Paul is speaking of created things like food, not of sin; the verse abolishes ritual defilement, not sin. Nor does it mean a believer should ignore a weaker brother’s conscience (Romans 14:13–21).

Does this mean I can watch or enjoy anything if my heart is pure? No. The verse is about created things good in themselves, food, drink, days, the material world, not things sinful in their nature or that feed sin in us. Pornography, cruelty and blasphemy are not made clean by a believer watching them, and a pure heart is the one that does not want to be stained by them (Philippians 4:8). A Christian is free to enjoy God’s good gifts with thanksgiving, not to call evil good. If you find yourself using this verse to quiet an uneasy conscience, that unease is worth listening to.

How do I get a clean conscience? Not by keeping more rules, but by the blood of Christ, which purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Bring your guilt to him by name; he is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse (1 John 1:9). Then believe him: you are clean. A conscience that keeps accusing you of forgiven sin needs Scripture’s teaching to rest in Christ’s finished work. Keep it clean by walking in the light and dealing with sin quickly. A conscience is a gift; keep it tender.

verseByVerse.quote: They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These teachers claim to know God, but their lives deny him, and that shows their claim is false: they are unfit for any good work.

They profess to know God. Not atheists: they make the claim openly, perhaps claiming special knowledge of God through their myths and rules.

But they deny him by their works. The verbs are set against each other deliberately: confessing and denying are the great opposites of the New Testament (Matthew 10:32–33). A man can confess with his mouth while denying with his life, and the life is what counts (1 John 2:4). An open opponent can be answered; a man who says all the right things while his life contradicts them is far harder to answer, and he is usually inside the church.

They are detestable. Three escalating words. “Detestable” is related to the Old Testament’s word for an abomination, used in the Greek Old Testament of idols and unclean things: men who talk endlessly about purity are pronounced unclean. “Disobedient” means refusing to be persuaded, the refusal to be ruled of verse 10.

Unfit for any good work. “Unfit” (adokimoi) is the word for metal tested and rejected (2 Timothy 3:8). The chapter ends where it began: real knowledge of God shows in a godly life (v. 1). It also opens a theme of the whole letter, devotion to good works (2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14), starting with men fit for none.

Lord, Lord. Jesus gave the sharpest commentary on this verse: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father”; to some who did mighty works in his name he will say, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:21–23). The Cretan teachers claimed to know God; the question at the last is whether God, in Christ, knows them. And that is the comfort for anyone frightened by this verse: knowing God is not finally a claim we make but a relationship he creates, and those the Son makes his own he also makes fit for good works (2:14).

Pure gold. One man’s works and words never once contradicted each other. Put to every test, in the wilderness, in Gethsemane, before Pilate and on the cross, he came out pure gold, and he gave himself for people who had failed every test. Now he sits as a refiner over the worthless metal of human lives and does not stop until it shines.

What it does not mean. It does not mean good works save. We are saved not by works but by mercy (3:5). But true saving faith always produces good works (Ephesians 2:10), and a profession which produces none has already been tested and failed.

In everyday life. The gap between Sunday’s words and Tuesday’s deeds is where this verse bites. Closing it is rarely dramatic: a debt paid, an apology made, a neighbour helped. And it is the fruit of Christ’s Spirit in you, not the price of his acceptance.

If I still sin a lot, am I denying God by my works? That the question troubles you is a good sign. Paul describes people whose lives as a whole contradict their profession, comfortable in disobedience, not believers who fight sin and often lose. Every Christian still sins (1 John 1:8); the difference is not perfection but direction. Do you hate your sin, confess it and keep returning to Christ? Are there good works in your life, however small, that come from love for him? Then you are not the man in this verse. Keep looking to Christ, whose righteousness covers you and whose Spirit is changing you.

What good works does God want from ordinary Christians? Mostly ordinary ones, done for his sake, as chapters 2 and 3 will show: loving your spouse and children, working honestly, self-control, submitting to rightful authorities, kindness and gentleness to everyone, help for those in urgent need, speaking evil of no one. God prepared them beforehand for us to walk in (Ephesians 2:10), so look for them where he has put you: your home, your street, your workplace, your church.

keyVerse.quote: He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.
keyVerse.note: The chapter moves from the God who never lies (v. 2) to the men who contradict his word (vv. 10–16), and this verse stands between them. The churches will be kept by leaders who cling to the word they were given, feeding the flock with health-giving teaching and guarding it from wolves. Their character makes the teaching believable; the word makes the character possible.

1.reflection:
Paul says the truth “accords with godliness” (v. 1), and the false teachers “deny him by their works” (v. 16). Where would someone who watched your week see the gap between what you believe and how you live?

Almost every quality required of elders (vv. 6–9) concerns character rather than gifting. Why do you think God sets it up that way, and how should it shape the way a church chooses, supports and prays for its leaders?

Titus is told to rebuke sharply (v. 13), Timothy to correct with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25). How can we tell which a situation needs, and what keeps any rebuke aimed at the other person’s health?

The first thing Paul says about God is that he “never lies” (v. 2). How does a God who has kept his word since before the ages began steady you in a world of spin, and in your own doubts?

2.title: Adorning the Doctrine: The Gospel-Shaped Community
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with teachers who profess to know God but deny him by their works (1:16). Chapter 2 gives the answer: what a church looks like when its life fits sound doctrine, and the grace that makes such a life possible.

The message. Sound doctrine has a shape, and it shows in ordinary lives: self-control, love at home, honest work, clean speech. The grace that appeared in Christ to save us is the same grace that trains us to live this way while we wait for him to appear in glory. Grace saves, and grace trains.

Why it was said. False teachers were overturning households (1:11), and outsiders watched the new faith closely, ready to blame it for broken homes and unreliable slaves (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Titus is to teach what fits sound doctrine (v. 1), group by group: older men, healthy in faith, love and endurance (v. 2); older women, reverent and teaching what is good (v. 3), training younger women to love their families and order their homes (vv. 4–5); younger men, self-control (v. 6), with Titus as their pattern (vv. 7–8); slaves, honesty and good faith (vv. 9–10). Each instruction carries a missionary reason: that the word of God is not reviled (v. 5), that opponents have nothing evil to say (v. 8), that slaves “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (v. 10). Then the reason underneath it all (vv. 11–14): grace has appeared, bringing salvation, and trains us to live godly lives now, as we wait for the appearing of our great God and Saviour, who gave himself to make a people zealous for good works. Titus must declare this with authority (v. 15).

Where it leads. The chapter stands between two appearings of Christ: grace appeared in a manger and on a cross, and glory will appear when he returns as “our great God and Savior”. The slave in a Cretan kitchen adorns the doctrine of a Saviour who himself took the form of a slave, and the King who paid for his people with himself calls a church of former liars and slaves his treasured possession.

For us. Ordinary faithfulness preaches. Ask what your home, your work and your tongue tell the neighbours about the gospel, and when you fail, go back to the grace that trains, not to grim resolve.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — What Accords With Sound Doctrine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church shows its doctrine is true by lives that fit it, and ordinary faithfulness makes the gospel attractive to outsiders. Titus is to teach each group what suits sound doctrine: older men, healthy faith, love and endurance (v. 2); older women, reverence and teaching what is good (v. 3), training younger women to love their families and order their homes (vv. 4–5); younger men, self-control (v. 6), with Titus as their pattern (vv. 7–8); slaves, honesty and good faith (vv. 9–10). Again and again the reason looks outward: that God’s word is not reviled, that critics have nothing to say, that the doctrine of God our Saviour is adorned.
verseByVerse.theology:
Doctrine Has a Shape

Titus is to teach what accords with sound doctrine (see the note on vv. 1–2). The high point is slaves making the doctrine of God our Saviour attractive (see the note on vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The only reason given for the household instructions is missionary: ‘that the word of God may not be reviled’ (v. 5).

Now: Older women are commanded to teach (see the notes on v. 3 and vv. 4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Titus must teach the way of life that fits sound doctrine, beginning with the older men, who are to stay clear-headed, worthy of respect and healthy in faith, love and endurance to the end.

But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. The contrast is with the empty talkers just described as unfit for any good work (1:10–16). “Accords with” means fitting, suitable. Titus must of course teach sound doctrine, but here he is told to teach what fits it: the way of life that sits on the truth as clothes fit a body. That is why for ten verses Paul teaches no doctrine, only conduct; and when the doctrine comes in verses 11–14, it turns out to be the reason for every line.

Older men are to be sober-minded. Paul begins with the group most likely to think itself exempt: not the elders but the older men of the congregation. “Sober-minded” means temperate, clear-headed (1 Timothy 3:2). Age brings its own temptations to excess, complacency or bitterness; older men must stay alert.

Dignified, self-controlled. Serious, worthy of respect; and sensible, sound-minded. Self-control is a keyword of this chapter (vv. 2, 4, 5, 6, 12).

Sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness. “Sound” is the medical word, healthy, describing here not doctrine but character: healthy faith, love and endurance. These are the familiar three (1 Corinthians 13:13) with steadfastness in place of hope, since steadfastness is hope under pressure. It belongs particularly to age: the old have had longest to learn it, and are most tempted to give up near the end.

Consider him who endured. Where does an old man find steadfastness for the last mile? “Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted” (Hebrews 12:3). Christian endurance is not gritted teeth but the patience of people whose eyes are fixed on a Saviour who finished his course. The older man who stays healthy in faith, love and steadfastness is not proving his own staying power; he is being kept by the one who, having loved his own, loved them to the end (John 13:1), and who promises that even to old age and grey hairs he will carry them (Isaiah 46:4).

In everyday life. Retirement can feel like being moved to the edge of things, in church as well as at work. Paul thinks otherwise: an older man who is still trusting, still loving and still going is one of the most persuasive sermons a congregation ever hears.

What are the particular dangers of growing old as a Christian? Cynicism: having seen churches split and leaders fall, it is easy to stop expecting God to do anything. Coldness: love shrinks to a small circle of the familiar. Bitterness over losses and disappointments. Complacency: thinking the battle with sin is over. Self-indulgence, when duties are fewer. And weariness, the temptation to stop serving and let the young get on with it. Paul’s three words answer them: healthy faith that still trusts, healthy love that still reaches out, healthy endurance that keeps going. Moses was eighty when God called him, and Caleb at eighty-five asked for a mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Older women are to carry themselves as people on holy ground, free of malicious talk and of slavery to drink, and to give themselves to teaching what is good.

Older women likewise are to be reverent. A temple word: carrying oneself as in a sacred place. An older Christian woman should move through ordinary life as though it were holy ground.

Not slanderers. Malicious gossips (diaboloi), the word used of the devil himself: a tongue that circulates accusations is doing the devil’s own work. The pull is often the pleasure of being in the know, which feels like importance. But knowing other people’s troubles is a trust to carry to God, not a currency to spend.

Or slaves to much wine. Held in settled bondage. Paul’s frankness is kind: a congregation that cannot name such things cannot help anyone caught in them. Gossip and drink tempt people with time on their hands and less to occupy them than they once had.

They are to teach what is good. One Greek word, teachers of good, found nowhere else in the Bible, and the cure for the two vices: Paul gives her a job. Not the public teaching office of elders (1 Timothy 2:12), but a powerful informal ministry, especially to younger women (v. 4), by word and example. Whatever 1 Timothy 2:12 means, it cannot mean women do not teach, because the man who wrote it commands them to.

The accuser and the advocate. Against the devil’s name stands one of Christ’s. Satan accuses our brothers day and night before our God (Revelation 12:10); but if anyone does sin, “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). The accuser tells our faults; the advocate covers them with his own blood. In every conversation a believer chooses which of the two to sound like, and one defended by Christ has every reason to defend others.

What it does not mean. It does not limit older women’s teaching to these topics or hearers; they rightly teach children (2 Timothy 1:5) and may explain the faith in many settings (Acts 18:26).

In everyday life. Many young mothers in a church are quietly overwhelmed, and few say so. An older woman who asks how she is really doing, and stays for the answer, may be the teacher of good Paul has in mind.

Does this mean Christians must not drink alcohol? No. The sin is being enslaved to wine, not using it. Wine is God’s gift to gladden the heart (Psalm 104:15); Jesus made it at a wedding (John 2:1–11), and Paul advised Timothy to take a little (1 Timothy 5:23). But Scripture plainly forbids drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), and some, for their own good or others’, will wisely not drink at all. If you find that you need a drink, hide how much you take, or others are worried, it may already have a hold on you. Tell someone, and get help; there is no shame in seeking freedom.

How can I tell the difference between sharing a concern and gossip? Ask who you are telling and why. Sharing is right when the hearer can help, or needs to know for someone’s protection, and you would be content for the person concerned to hear what you said. Gossip passes on faults or troubles to people who cannot help, for the interest of the story or to make yourself look better. Have I spoken to the person first (Matthew 18:15)? Would I say this to their face? When in doubt, pray about it instead of talking about it.

verseByVerse.quote: and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Older women are to train younger wives in warm love for husband and children, in purity, kindness and a well-run home, and in willingly following their own husbands, so that no one has cause to speak evil of God’s word.

And so train the young women. This passage troubles modern readers most, so read it exactly. “Train” means to teach to be sensible, the root of self-controlled. The older women train the younger, not Titus, which also keeps a male minister out of the private dealings with young wives that 1 Timothy 5:2 guards so carefully.

To love their husbands and children. Two more single Greek words, husband-loving and child-loving, using the word for warm affection. These are taught: Paul does not assume affection arrives automatically with marriage and motherhood, or that a woman struggling there is defective. Such love can be learned, from someone further along and from the Spirit, through whom God’s love has been poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5).

To be self-controlled, pure. Sensible, and chaste: morally clean and sexually faithful.

Working at home, kind. Busy at home (some manuscripts read keepers of the home): managing the household diligently (1 Timothy 5:14; Proverbs 31:10–31), unlike the idle younger widows of 1 Timothy 5:13. The household was a productive economic unit, and a competent wife ran a small business. “Kind” means good and generous, the quality that makes a busy home a refuge.

And submissive to their own husbands. A willing placing of oneself under: the wife’s respectful following of her husband’s loving leadership (Ephesians 5:22–33; Colossians 3:18; 1 Peter 3:1–6). The qualifier, often dropped, matters: “their own husbands”. Paul is not putting women as a class under men as a class, but speaking of a marriage. And it sits beside the command that husbands love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), a demand that, if anything, costs more.

That the word of God may not be reviled. If Christian wives abandoned their families or flouted their husbands, outsiders would blame the gospel. New religions were already suspected of breaking up households: a respectable wife was expected to worship her husband’s gods (so Plutarch, advising a bride and groom), and a Christian wife, above all one married to an unbeliever, was closely watched (1 Peter 3:1–2).

A marriage that preaches. Why should a young wife’s home affect what pagans think of the word of God? Because marriage was made to picture Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32). A Christian home is a small sermon preached without words. When it is cold, chaotic or cruel, the sermon tells lies about Christ; when husband and wife love each other in that pattern, the watching town sees in miniature the love of the Bridegroom for his bride.

He provided for his mother from the cross. The Son of God grew up subject to his parents in an ordinary home, and from the cross, in agony, he provided for his mother (Luke 2:51; John 19:26–27). No household duty is beneath the Lord who honoured one. And every home ordered in love points to the wedding all the others foreshadow, when the Lamb’s bride sits down at his supper; married or single, every believer has a place at that table.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid women to work outside the home; the excellent wife of Proverbs 31 trades, buys land and sells goods. It means the home is not neglected. Nor does submission imply inferiority: Christ submits to the Father, yet is equal with him (1 Corinthians 15:28). And it does not apply to single women, whose calling is equally honourable.

Must a wife submit to an abusive husband? No. Submission is given to a husband in his proper role, as to the Lord; it never means joining in sin, or enduring violence, threats or control. A husband who abuses his wife has abandoned the very headship he claims, which Scripture defines as giving himself up for her. A wife in danger should seek safety and help at once, and the church and the law should protect her (Romans 13:4); leaders must never send her back into harm in the name of submission or reconciliation. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to the desertion that Scripture accepts as a ground for divorce (1 Corinthians 7:15; the Westminster Confession 24.5–6), and the elders should help judge her case with her. Abuse is never to be tolerated; the church’s first duty is to the vulnerable.

What does submission look like in an ordinary Christian marriage? A wife who respects her husband, supports his leadership, speaks well of him, and will follow his lead when, after honest discussion, they cannot agree. It does not mean she has no opinions or does all the work; a wise husband seeks her counsel. And it is matched by a husband who leads by serving: taking responsibility, praying with his family, putting his wife’s good before his own, listening, never using his headship to get his own way. When both walk with Christ, it feels like partnership with an order to it.

Where Christians differ: does this teach a fixed role for wives in every culture? Egalitarians (who hold that Scripture assigns no distinct roles to husband and wife) argue that Paul is accommodating to first-century culture to avoid offence, and that in another culture mutual submission without distinct roles would better adorn the gospel. This commentary’s view: the motive is indeed partly missional (vv. 5, 8, 10). But elsewhere Paul grounds the wife’s submission in Christ’s relationship with the church (Ephesians 5:22–33) and in creation (1 Corinthians 11:8–9), which do not change with culture. This is the complementarian view: husbands and wives are equal in dignity and worth, with distinct and complementary roles; the husband leads with self-sacrificing love like Christ, and the wife follows with respect and strength. It never means a wife must obey a command to sin (Acts 5:29), endure abuse, or lose her voice and gifts. Egalitarian Christians reach their view out of the same wish to honour Scripture and adorn the gospel, and this commentary counts them brothers and sisters.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Young men need above all to master themselves, and Titus must show them how by a life and teaching so clean that opponents have nothing true to say against the church.

Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. One instruction, the word already given to older men and younger women (vv. 2, 5), and it covers everything. Young men are prone to impulsiveness, anger, lust, pride and recklessness; sound judgment and self-mastery are what they most need (2 Timothy 2:22).

A model of good works. Then Titus himself. “Model” (typos) is a stamp or mould: he is not merely to teach this chapter; his own life is to be the pattern others are shaped by.

And in your teaching show integrity, dignity. “Integrity” means teaching with no self-interest mixed in. On an island of men teaching for shameful gain (1:11), that was the visible difference. With it goes dignity, treating the things of God with the seriousness they deserve.

Sound speech that cannot be condemned. A healthy word, beyond criticism: not speech nobody dislikes, but speech that gives no fair ground for complaint.

So that an opponent may be put to shame. Paul assumes there will be opponents; he aims not at being liked but at giving them nothing true to work with. A church that is attacked is no disgrace; a church that has handed its attackers the ammunition is.

Having nothing evil to say about us. Us: what a young minister on Crete does will be blamed on the whole gospel cause, the apostle included. A blameless life silences critics (1 Peter 2:12, 15).

The speech no one could condemn. The standard had already been met once. When the chief priests sought testimony against Jesus to put him to death, they found none; the false witnesses did not agree (Mark 14:55–56). Every teacher who aims at sound speech follows the one who left us an example (1 Peter 2:21). But Titus would sometimes fail and need forgiving; Christ never did, and it is his blameless life, not ours, on which our standing rests.

He mastered what young men cannot. Christ did his work as a young man. Hungry in the wilderness, he would not turn stones into bread; offered the kingdoms of the world, he would not bow; mocked on the cross, he would not come down. And he gives his Spirit, whose fruit is self-control, to young men who cannot master themselves.

What does self-control look like for a young man today? Mastering the appetites before they master you. Guarding your eyes and your screen against pornography, with accountability if you need it (Job 31:1). Controlling your temper, online and in traffic. Managing money instead of spending on impulse. Treating women as sisters, in all purity (1 Timothy 5:2). Getting up and doing your work. Thinking before you speak. None of it is possible by willpower alone; it is the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23). But the Spirit works through your choices, so make them, and find an older man to walk with you.

Do I have to be perfect before I can set an example? No; neither Titus nor Paul was. A model of good works is someone whose life as a whole shows what following Christ looks like, including how to repent. Often the most helpful example a younger believer sees is an older one confessing a sin, apologising and starting again. What disqualifies is hypocrisy, teaching one thing and living another without shame. Aim at consistency, not perfection, and when your life and words part company, say so and put it right.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian slaves are to serve honestly and faithfully, so that their lives make the teaching about God our Saviour beautiful to those who watch them.

Bondservants are to be submissive. The last group: slaves. “In everything” means in all that does not require sin (Acts 5:29).

They are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative. Well-pleasing is doing their work well. “Argumentative” means talking back, the constant low-level resistance of the powerless; it is the word used of the false teachers who contradict the truth (1:9).

Not pilfering. Secretly keeping back for oneself, the word used of Ananias keeping back part of the money (Acts 5:2–3). Petty theft was so common that many hardly thought it stealing. Paul does.

But showing all good faith. Complete trustworthiness. Picture an owner who finds that things have stopped going missing and his slave has stopped answering back, and who cannot explain it.

That they may adorn the doctrine. The reason gives the lowliest people in the church a remarkable dignity. “Adorn” (kosmōsin, the root of cosmetic) means to set in order and make beautiful, as a setting shows a jewel at its best. Slaves who could be beaten at will are told that their honesty in small things displays the doctrine of God at its best. The doctrine is already true; their lives display its beauty.

What Paul does and does not do. Paul is not endorsing the institution. He lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), tells masters they answer to a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1), most likely tells a slave to take freedom if he can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and sends a runaway back as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). Here he tells people with no legal power how to live with dignity inside a system they cannot change.

The setting for the jewel. At the centre of the doctrine of God our Saviour is a Saviour who took the form of a servant, a doulos, and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:7–8). He washed feet, was sold for the price of a slave, did not answer back when reviled, and kept nothing back for himself. The gospel was not stooping when it came into the kitchens of Crete; it was coming home to the kind of life the Son of God had chosen. When a man who could pilfer stops pilfering, he looks, in a small way, like the one he trusts, and the most powerless people on the island become the setting in which the jewel is shown.

In everyday life. Pilfering rarely feels like theft now either: ten minutes taken here, a padded claim there. Stopping it will probably go unnoticed, but it is exactly the small honesty that makes the doctrine of God beautiful.

Why didn’t Paul simply condemn slavery? He was writing to a tiny, powerless minority with no means of abolishing it, about how to live where they were. But he planted the seeds that destroyed it: slave and master are brothers, equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28), and where the gospel took hold Christians came in time to see that the institution could not stand beside it. The Atlantic slave trade, built on kidnapping and race, was condemned by Scripture from the start: stealing a person to sell him was a capital crime in the law of Moses (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10). To their shame, many professing Christians defended it anyway; others, reading the same Bible, led the fight to end it.

Does this mean I must obey my boss in everything? The principles apply to employees, with a difference: you chose your job and can leave it. Be diligent, respectful, honest and reliable, even with a difficult manager (1 Peter 2:18). Do not talk back, take home what is not yours, pad your hours or expenses, or quietly do less than you are paid for. But no employer may require sin: falsifying records, deceiving customers, cutting corners on safety, covering up wrongdoing. There obey God rather than men, respectfully, and accept the cost.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace is the reason under every household duty: the grace that appeared in Christ to save us also trains us. It has appeared, bringing salvation to all kinds of people (v. 11), and teaches us to say no to ungodliness and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives now (v. 12), as we wait for the appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ (v. 13). He gave himself to redeem and purify a people of his own, eager to do good (v. 14). Titus must declare it with authority and let no one disregard him (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Our Great God and Saviour Jesus Christ

In the Greek of verse 13, ‘our great God and Saviour’ is one person, Jesus Christ (see the note on v. 13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Grace appeared to all kinds of people, the slave on the same terms as the master (see the note on v. 11).

Now: Grace is the teacher (v. 12). A people eager for good works is what Christ’s redeeming death produces, not what pays for it (see the note on vv. 14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s grace has broken into the world in Jesus Christ, bringing salvation to every kind of person, and that is the reason behind every instruction in verses 1–10.

For the grace of God has appeared. “For”: after ten verses of household instruction comes the reason underneath them, a summary of the gospel as rich as any Paul wrote, given to explain why an older woman should not gossip and a slave should not pilfer. “Has appeared” is the shining-out word, used of the sun breaking through (Luke 1:78–79) and of a king making a public appearance. Grace was not merely announced; it showed up in a person, in Jesus Christ’s birth, life, death and resurrection (John 1:14). The tense is past and definite: an event you could have attended, in Bethlehem, in Galilee, outside Jerusalem.

Bringing salvation. Grace does not merely offer salvation; it brings it: not a possibility held out but a rescue carried in.

For all people. After old men, old women, young women, young men and slaves (vv. 2–10), “all people” means all kinds of people, an answer to false teachers who ranked people in higher and lower grades. Grace has appeared to the slave in the kitchen on exactly the same terms as to the master.
