Grace has a birthday. For ages it lay hidden in the heart of God, promised and foreshadowed; then it dawned over a manger, a carpenter’s bench, the roads of Galilee and a hill outside Jerusalem. And Paul does not say: behave well, and then grace may appear. He says behave well because it already has.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all people will be saved; Scripture teaches eternal judgment for those who reject Christ (Matthew 7:13–14; 25:46).

If grace is for all kinds of people, can I tell anyone that Christ will save them? Yes, and you should. The gospel is offered freely and sincerely to every person, with the promise that whoever believes in Christ will be saved (John 3:16; Romans 10:13). You need not know whether someone is elect; God has bound himself to save everyone who comes, and no background, class, race or past puts anyone beyond this grace. Tell them that Christ receives sinners, and urge them to come.

Where Christians differ: does grace bring salvation to everyone without exception? Some read this verse as teaching that God’s grace makes salvation equally available to every individual, or even that all will be saved. This commentary’s view: the context shows that “all people” means all kinds and classes of people, those listed in verses 2–10, as in 1 Timothy 2:4–6. And grace that brings salvation actually saves: it trains those it saves (v. 12), and Christ redeemed a particular people for his own possession (v. 14). This fits definite atonement (Christ died to secure the salvation of a particular people) and effectual grace (grace that actually brings a person to faith), while the gospel is still freely offered to everyone. Christians who read the verse more broadly usually share the same eagerness to offer Christ to all.

Uncertain wording. The Greek is compressed: “for all people” could go with “bringing salvation” (salvation for all people), as in the ESV and most modern translations, or with “has appeared” (grace has appeared to all people), as in the KJV. The meaning changes little: either way, the context shows that “all” means people of every kind, slave and master alike.

verseByVerse.quote: training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace that saves us also trains us, teaching us to refuse ungodliness and sinful desire and to live sensible, just and devout lives here and now.

Training us. The word for raising a child (compare 2 Timothy 3:16). Grace not only pardons but teaches, in a lifelong school.

To renounce ungodliness. To say no to, decisively; the verb used of Peter denying Christ. Ungodliness is irreverence, the root sin: living as if God did not matter.

And worldly passions. Desires belonging to this world in its rebellion against God: lust, greed, pride, envy (1 John 2:15–17). Not desire as such, which God made, but desire bent toward what the world offers in place of him.

Self-controlled, upright, and godly lives. Three words facing three directions: sensibly (the chapter’s word once more), inward; justly, outward toward others; reverently, upward toward God. No part of life is left out.

In the present age. Not in retreat from it or when circumstances improve, but on Crete, now, among the liars.

Grace does the teaching. Anyone who has heard that too much grace produces loose living should weigh this verse. Paul does not balance grace with law; grace itself does the teaching, and does it better, because a rule can stop a man stealing but cannot make him stop wanting what is not his. Grace gives a new heart, with God’s law written on it (Jeremiah 31:33). A man who knows he is forgiven and loved at infinite cost does not want to go on wounding the one who loved him.

The life grace is shaping. Self-controlled, upright and godly in the present age describes one life that has already been lived. The Son of God was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15); he refused every worldly passion the devil offered, dealt justly with every person he met, and lived every hour in communion with his Father. Grace is not training us to match a set of ideals but making us like the Son (Romans 8:29), whose righteousness is already counted as ours.

The new Stoics. Self-control is fashionable again. Marcus Aurelius sells in airport bookshops, and podcasts promise a mastered self: early mornings, cold water, fewer distractions. Much of it is wiser than the drift it replaces, and Paul would recognise the vocabulary. But the Stoic masters himself by his own reason, for the sake of a self that is calm and untouchable, and the project ends one of two ways: you succeed and quietly despise the undisciplined, or you fail and despise yourself. Pride or despair are the moralist’s two fates. Paul’s self-control has a different engine and goal: it is taught by grace, which no one earns, and it looks towards the appearing of Christ (v. 13). So the one who falls can get up without self-loathing, and the one who succeeds has nothing to boast of. Discipline stops being a way of saving yourself and becomes a way of loving the one who saved you.

What it does not mean. Not that grace makes effort unnecessary: grace trains, and we learn; grace empowers, and we work (Philippians 2:12–13). Nor that we will be perfect in this age, but that we will grow.

How does grace actually train me? Through the means God has appointed, used in the light of the cross: Scripture, showing what God loves and hates; preaching, which applies it; the Lord’s Supper, which sets Christ’s sacrifice before your eyes; prayer; the church, where others encourage and correct you; and providence, including hard things, by which God disciplines his children for their good (Hebrews 12:10–11). Under all of it, grace trains by changing what you love: the more you see of Christ’s kindness, the less you want what he died to free you from.

What does saying no look like when temptation comes? A decision made in advance and acted on quickly. Know your weak points and plan: what you will not look at, where you will not go, what you will do instead. When temptation comes, do not argue with it; turn from it, as Joseph ran (Genesis 39:12). Pray at once, even one sentence. Remind yourself: I am not a slave to this any more; Christ died to free me from it. Replace it with something good. And if you fall, do not wallow; confess, receive forgiveness and get up. Grace that says no to sin also says yes to the sinner who returns.

verseByVerse.quote: waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians live waiting for the return of Jesus Christ in glory, and Paul names him plainly as “our great God and Savior”. The one we wait for is God himself.

Waiting for our blessed hope. Grace appeared (v. 11); glory will appear (v. 13); the whole chapter is lived between the two. Waiting is eager welcoming, not idleness (2 Timothy 4:8), and hope is certain expectation.

The appearing of the glory. “Appearing” is the usual word for Christ’s return (2 Timothy 4:1), from the verb of verse 11: grace has shone out, and glory will shine out. Not merely a glorious appearing, but the appearing of the glory itself (Matthew 25:31): the first time he came hidden in flesh; next time the glory will be unveiled.

Of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. Is Paul naming one person or two: the great God and also our Saviour, or one great God and Saviour who is Jesus Christ? In Greek a single “the” stands before both titles: tou megalou theou kai sōtēros hēmōn Iēsou Christou. By a well-known rule of Greek grammar, often called Granville Sharp’s rule, when one “the” covers two singular titles joined by “and”, and neither is a personal name, both describe the same person. Moreover, it is Christ, not the Father, whose appearing the New Testament expects. The same construction appears in 2 Peter 1:1, and other passages also call Jesus God (John 1:1; 20:28; Hebrews 1:8).

The argument closes. The letter calls now God, now Christ, our Saviour (1:3, 4; 2:10, 13; 3:4, 6), and here completes the case: the Saviour is God. That lifts the chapter’s ordinary instructions into a startling light: the slave not pilfering in a Cretan kitchen adorns the doctrine of God our Saviour (v. 10), and this God and Saviour is the man who died for him.

The great God in a manger. The baby in the manger at Bethlehem is the great God. The man who wept at Lazarus’s tomb is the great God. The one who hung on the cross, mocked and bleeding, is the great God and our Saviour. And when he comes again in the glory he had with the Father before the world existed, those who have loved his appearing will see his face, and their waiting will turn to sight.

What it does not mean. Calling Jesus our great God does not erase the distinction between him and the Father. They are distinct persons, both fully God.

How do I wait for Christ’s appearing in practice? By living in a way that would be glad to be interrupted by him. Keep short accounts with God and others. Hold possessions loosely, and spend your life on what will last: people, the gospel, good works. Pray, as the church always has, come, Lord Jesus. Let the hope steady you in suffering, because the present age is not the last word. Do not waste energy on date-setting; he has told us to be ready, not to calculate. The best preparation for his appearing is the life of verse 12.

Is our blessed hope a secret rapture before a tribulation? No. Paul names the hope: one glorious, visible appearing. Scripture describes Christ’s coming as public, like lightning across the sky (Matthew 24:27), with a shout and a trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16), when every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). At that one coming the dead will be raised, believers gathered to meet him, the wicked judged, and all things made new. Christians will face trouble before then, as they always have; their hope is not escape from the world but the return of its King. Many sincere believers have been taught a pre-tribulation rapture and share the same longing for Christ; this commentary reads these passages as one coming because each is public and loud, and the difference is no reason for division between brothers.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus called God here? Some, including Jehovah’s Witnesses and some older scholars, translate “the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (the KJV wording), as two persons, the Father and the Son, though the KJV translators may well have meant one. This commentary’s view: the grammar, the context, and the New Testament’s consistent expectation of Christ’s (not the Father’s) appearing all support “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ”, the reading of most modern translations and of the early Greek church fathers, who spoke Greek as their native language. Christ is fully God, equal with the Father, one God in three persons.
verseByVerse.note: One of the clearest New Testament statements that Jesus is God.

verseByVerse.quote: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ gave himself to buy his people out of every kind of sin and to make them his own treasured people, clean and eager to do good; Titus must declare this with full authority.

Who gave himself for us. In the same breath as his highest statement that Christ is God, Paul speaks of the cross. The giving is voluntary (Galatians 2:20), the whole person handed over, and “for us” means in our place: substitution, the heart of the gospel.

To redeem us from all lawlessness. “Redeem” means to set free by paying a price, the language of buying a slave’s freedom (Mark 10:45), which the slaves in the congregation would hear with longing. “All lawlessness” is every kind of sin (1 John 3:4), nothing left unbought: Christ’s death frees us from sin’s penalty (justification) and from its power (sanctification). Psalm 130:8 promised that God himself would redeem Israel from all its iniquities; here the great God does it.

And to purify for himself a people. Christ died not only to forgive but to make his people clean and holy (Ephesians 5:25–27). For himself: he is not cleaning them for someone else; he wants them.

For his own possession. A treasured possession, echoing God’s words to Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5). The church of Jews and Gentiles is God’s treasured people, the true Israel (1 Peter 2:9–10); Christians differ on whether God also has a future purpose for the Jewish people (Romans 11:25–29), but not on this.

Who are zealous for good works. Eager, passionate. The order is everything: he gave himself, redeemed, purified, took possession, and the result is a people eager to do good. The works are not the price of the possession but what possession produces (Ephesians 2:10). So the chapter ends where chapter 1 ended, on good works, with the opposite verdict: the false teachers were unfit for any (1:16); Christ’s people are zealous for them.

Declare these things; exhort and rebuke. “These things” gathers up the whole chapter: announce, encourage, correct. “With all authority” is the authority of God’s word, not Titus’s own.

Let no one disregard you. To look past or look down on. Timothy was not to let anyone despise his youth (1 Timothy 4:12); Titus is not to be ignored. He cannot control what people think of him, only whether he gives them grounds (vv. 7–8): he has the authority of God’s word and must not throw it away by the way he lives.

A King who paid with himself. Kings collect treasure they never paid for with themselves. This King gave himself. The great God walked into the slave market of sin, where we stood with nothing to offer, and bought us with his own life, not to set us to work in his fields at a distance but to bring us into his house as his own. He looks at a scatter of Cretan congregations, slaves and former liars among them, and calls them his treasured possession, and he means it.

What it does not mean. “All authority” does not license harshness or domineering; his authority is the message’s.

Did Christ die for everyone, or only for his people? This verse says he gave himself to redeem and purify a people for his own possession, and the purpose was achieved. Reformed Christians therefore hold that Christ’s death was designed to save his elect and actually secures their salvation, rather than making salvation possible for all and certain for none (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). Other evangelicals believe Christ died for every person in the same way. All agree that his death is of infinite worth, sufficient for the whole world, and that the gospel must be offered to everyone. What definite atonement adds is the certainty that the cross did not fail: everyone Christ died for will be his.

If I am not zealous for good works, am I really his? Zeal grows; it does not arrive full-grown. If you trust Christ and want to please him, even feebly, that desire is the beginning of what this verse describes. Feed it: think often about what Christ gave for you, because zeal is kindled by gratitude, not guilt; spend time with believers eager to do good, for zeal is contagious; start small and practical. But if you feel no desire at all to please God, and are content to be so, take that seriously and go to Christ honestly about it. He does not reject the cold who come to him; he warms them.
verseByVerse.note: “A people for his own possession” echoes God’s words to Israel at Sinai.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine.<sup>2</sup>Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.<sup>3</sup>Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good,<sup>4</sup>and so train the young women to love their husbands and children,<sup>5</sup>to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled.<sup>6</sup>Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled.<sup>7</sup>Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity,<sup>8</sup>and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.<sup>9</sup>Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative,<sup>10</sup>not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.<sup>11</sup>For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,<sup>12</sup>training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,<sup>13</sup>waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,<sup>14</sup>who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works.<sup>15</sup>Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you.

keyVerse.quote: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works.
keyVerse.note: Every instruction in the chapter, from the older man’s steadiness to the slave’s honesty, is a good work, and this verse says where good works come from. Christ gave himself to buy his people out of sin and make them his own, and a people eager to do good is the fruit of that redemption, never its price. It is the exact opposite of the false teachers, “unfit for any good work” (1:16).

2.reflection:
Most of the instructions in verses 1–10 come with a reason that looks outward (vv. 5, 8, 10). What might your neighbours or colleagues conclude about the gospel from watching your home, your work and your speech this past month?

Paul wants older believers to teach and train the younger (vv. 2–5). Who has done that for you, and whom could you walk alongside now?

Verses 11–12 say that grace itself trains us to say no to ungodliness. How is being trained by grace different from trying harder or keeping rules, and where do you most need that training?

Christ “gave himself for us” (v. 14), and Paul calls him “our great God and Savior” (v. 13). How does seeing who he is and what he paid change the way you think about ordinary, unnoticed obedience?

3.title: Heirs of Hope: Conduct in Society and the Gospel's Foundation
3.overview:
Where we are. After elders set in place against false teachers (chapter 1) and each group in the church taught how to live by the grace that has appeared (chapter 2), Paul turns outward, to life among unbelieving rulers and neighbours, and then closes with a warning about quarrels, travel plans and grace.

The message. People saved by God’s kindness alone are to show kindness to everyone. God met us, when we were foolish, enslaved and hateful, not with contempt but with mercy, so we can be gentle, courteous and useful to the people around us, including those who are still what we once were. Free grace is not the enemy of good works; it is the reason for them.

Why it was said. The Cretan churches were young, on an island known for unrest and dishonesty, watched by suspicious neighbours and troubled by teachers who loved quarrels about the law (see the introduction). Believers could easily drift into rebellion, into superiority over their neighbours, or into endless argument.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul sets out the conduct of good citizens (vv. 1–2). Then the reason: we ourselves were once no better (v. 3), until God our Saviour appeared and saved us by his own mercy, through the Spirit’s washing and renewal, so that, justified by grace, we are heirs of eternal life (vv. 4–7). Titus must insist on this, so that believers devote themselves to good works (v. 8). By contrast, quarrels about genealogies and the law are worthless, and a divisive man is to be warned twice and then refused (vv. 9–11). Even the closing errands become a lesson in meeting urgent needs (vv. 12–14). Grace has the last word (v. 15).

Where it leads. Verses 4–7 are among the richest summaries of salvation in Scripture, and the whole Trinity is in them: the Father’s kindness appearing, the Spirit poured out richly, through Jesus Christ our Saviour. God’s love for mankind took a human face and came down into the street where people were hating one another, and instead of destroying them he washed them. The hope of eternal life with which the letter began (1:2) is ours because it is Christ’s inheritance, shared with his people.

For us. Ask how you speak of the people you find hardest to respect, in public life or next door, and remember what you were. Then let the grace that saved you set you to work, planning good for others instead of winning arguments.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — He Saved Us, Not Because of Works
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers can be gentle with everyone because God was kind to them when they deserved nothing. Paul asks for good citizenship and courtesy toward all (vv. 1–2), and grounds it in memory: we ourselves were once foolish, enslaved and hateful (v. 3). Then comes one of the Bible’s fullest summaries of salvation: God our Saviour appeared and saved us by his mercy alone, through the Spirit’s washing and renewal, so that, justified by grace, we are heirs of eternal life (vv. 4–7; on the whole Trinity at work in it, see vv. 6–7). Titus must insist on this, because free grace is what makes people devoted to good works (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as the Engine of Works

Having excluded even our righteous works from the reason we are saved (v.5), Paul says to insist on that doctrine precisely so that believers devote themselves to good works (see the note on v. 8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a province prone to unrest, submission to authorities was the Christian's default posture (v.1; cf. Acts 5:29).

Now: Courtesy toward the ungodly comes from an accurate memory: ‘we ourselves were once’ (v.3).

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians are to be good citizens and good neighbours: willing under authority, ready to help, and gentle toward everyone.

Remind them. Keep reminding them: much of a minister’s work, and of the Christian life, is remembering what we already know.

To be submissive to rulers and authorities. To order themselves under civil government, which God has instituted for order and justice (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). Crete was known for unruliness, and the churches probably included Jewish converts (1:10) from communities that resented Rome; a movement suspected of stirring up revolt could easily have been crushed. And, as in 2:5, 8 and 10, the gospel’s good name was at stake: quiet, useful lives would commend the teaching about God our Saviour to suspicious neighbours (1 Peter 2:12, 15).

To be obedient. In all that does not require sin (Acts 5:29). Submission is the normal attitude to rightful authority, not a promise to do whatever one is told (on authority in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21).

To be ready for every good work. Good works, the letter’s refrain, here mean being useful to the community, not just avoiding trouble (Jeremiah 29:7; Galatians 6:10). Christians are to be the people a town is glad to have in it.

To speak evil of no one, to avoid quarrelling, to be gentle. Not to slander or revile anyone, rulers, pagan neighbours and opponents included. “Avoid quarrelling” is literally not a fighter, the requirement for an overseer (1 Timothy 3:3). “Gentle” is hard to translate: gracious, reasonable, yielding, the person who does not insist on the last inch of his rights.

And to show perfect courtesy toward all people. Literally all meekness toward all people: every kind of gentleness toward every kind of person, unbelievers and enemies included. Paul knows how demanding that is, so he gives the reason at once (v. 3).

The meekness and gentleness of Christ. Gentleness and meekness are a pair Paul uses of one person: he appealed to the Corinthians “by the meekness and gentleness of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:1), and Jesus said, “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The courtesy asked of Cretan believers is Christ’s own character reproduced in his people. They are to treat a sneering official or a hostile neighbour as their Lord treated Pilate and the soldiers, with a gentleness that is not weakness, because it comes from someone who is not afraid.

That throne is already occupied. Over every magistrate in Crete, and over Caesar in Rome, stood a higher throne, and the one seated on it had been executed under a Roman governor. Yet he rules as no Caesar ever ruled: a bruised reed he will not break (Isaiah 42:3). Because that throne is already occupied, his people need neither fear their rulers nor despise them. They can be gentle with the whole world, as their King has been gentle with them.

What does courtesy toward all people look like? A gentle manner kept up with people who give you no reason for it. You answer the curt email more calmly than you were spoken to, speak of the absent as if they were in the room, and let someone else have the last word in an argument that does not matter. You notice the people most easily overlooked, the cleaner, the newcomer, the person on the edge of the conversation, because to God they matter. And when you fail, you apologise without a speech in your own defence. None of this comes from gritting your teeth, but from remembering verses 3 to 5: God met us, foolish and hateful, with “goodness and loving kindness”.

How should a Christian speak about politicians he disagrees with? Truthfully, but without contempt. You may say plainly that a policy is unjust, that a leader has lied, or that a law contradicts God’s word; the prophets did. But you may not mock, curse, spread rumours, or speak of anyone as beneath respect. Pray for them by name (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Before you post or repeat something, ask whether it is true, whether it is kind, and whether you would say it to their face. Paul wrote this under Nero. If courtesy was owed to him, it is owed to the people in office now, of every party.

When must a Christian refuse to obey the government? When it commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands. The apostles refused to stop preaching (Acts 5:29); Daniel kept praying (Daniel 6:10); the Hebrew midwives refused to kill babies (Exodus 1:17). Even then, refuse respectfully and openly, accept the lawful penalty, and do not turn to violence or deceit. In free societies you may also work to change bad laws by lawful means: voting, petitioning, speaking, standing for office. What you may not do is treat every law you dislike as an excuse to ignore authority altogether.

verseByVerse.quote: For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians can be gentle with outsiders because they remember that they were once just like them.

For we ourselves were once. Not “they were” but “we ourselves”. Paul, the former Pharisee who by the law’s standard had been blameless (Philippians 3:6), places himself among the foolish and enslaved without qualification. Humility is the root of gentleness.

Foolish, disobedient, led astray. Seven items follow, going steadily downward: spiritually blind (Ephesians 4:18), refusing to be persuaded (1:16), and led astray, which is passive: we did not only wander; we were led, deceived by sin and Satan.

Slaves to various passions and pleasures. Our appetites owned us, though we thought we were free (Romans 6:16–20).

Passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another. Not occasional lapses but the air a whole life was lived in, and a whole society: everyone despising and being despised.

An accurate memory. How do you show perfect courtesy to people who are foolish, enslaved and hateful? By remembering that the description is your own. Contempt for the ungodly, the easy sin of moral and religious people, is not defeated by trying harder to be patient, but by an accurate memory. The Cretan liar is not a different species from the man teaching him. He is at a stage his teacher has been through, and only the kindness and mercy of God our Saviour moved the teacher out of it.

If the Son sets you free. Jesus gave the same diagnosis, with its cure: everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin, and if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36). And the hatred at the bottom of the list was met by a love that ran the other way. Christ was hated without a cause (John 15:25), and he died for those who hated him while they were still his enemies (Romans 5:10). He was hated without a cause so that hateful people could be loved without a cause.

What it does not mean. Not that every unbeliever is as bad as he could be outwardly, or does nothing good in a civil sense. Apart from grace, every part of human nature is corrupted by sin and unable to turn to God (Romans 3:10–18; 8:7–8): not that we are as wicked as possible, but that we cannot save ourselves.

If I was raised a Christian, does this describe me? Yes, though it may not feel like it. Paul was raised in the most careful religious home imaginable and still put himself in this list. You may never have been a drunkard or a thief, but the root of this verse is in every heart: blindness to God, a will that resists him, desires that rule us, envy and pride, which a respectable life can hide even from ourselves. You need not invent a dramatic past, only see your heart as God sees it, and know that you too were saved only by mercy. That will keep you gentle with people whose sins are louder than yours.

How do I stop feeling superior to unbelievers? Remember, regularly and specifically, what you were and would still be without grace; the difference was made by God, not by you (1 Corinthians 4:7). Get to know unbelievers as people, not categories, and you will often find kindness, honesty and wisdom in them that rebuke you. Pray for them, one face at a time; it is very hard to despise someone you are praying for. And keep looking at the cross, where Christ died for the ungodly, which includes you.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God saved us because he is kind and merciful, not because of anything we had done, by his Spirit washing us clean and making us new.

But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Saviour appeared. Into the hatred of verse 3, something appeared. “Loving kindness” is literally philanthropy, love for mankind. The Greeks praised rulers for their philanthropy; Paul says the true philanthropy is God’s, shown to the very people just described. “Appeared” is the verb of 2:11, and in both places Paul means the coming of Jesus Christ.

He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness. The saving is complete, and God did it. Not merely bad works are ruled out, but the best things we ever did, religious ones included (Ephesians 2:8–9). That is harder for a decent person to hear than for a scoundrel. A salvation we could take some credit for would leave us still in charge and God slightly in our debt; mercy leaves room only for thanks.

But according to his own mercy. The whole cause is on God’s side: mercy is shown to the wretched, not the deserving. It is not the holy God relaxing his law; he can show mercy to the guilty and still be just, because his Son bore the judgment they deserved (Romans 3:25–26).

By the washing of regeneration. “Regeneration” (palingenesia) is literally genesis again: a new beginning, not a repaired old one. The new birth is a cleansing from sin, as in Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises clean water, a new heart and a new spirit. The word appears elsewhere only in Matthew 19:28, of the renewal of the whole world: the God who has begun that new creation in his people will finish it.

And renewal of the Holy Spirit. Washing and renewal are both the Spirit’s work, and neither is ours (see Uncertain wording below). The new birth happens once; the renewing goes on throughout life (Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 4:16).

Love for mankind in a human face. God’s love for humanity did not stay a feeling in heaven: the Son took our nature and died for people who were foolish, enslaved and hateful. Not a ruler’s gift handed out from a palace, but the King himself coming down into the street. The lover of mankind looked on people hating one another and did not destroy them; he washed them. The Spirit’s washing applies what the Son came to do.

What it does not mean. Not that regeneration is a reward for faith. It is God’s work in the dead sinner, which produces faith (John 1:12–13; Ephesians 2:4–5).

In everyday life. Write down, in one sentence, why God saved you. If anything in it is about you, cross it out and try again, and let what is left turn into thanks.

If baptism does not save, why be baptised? Because Christ commands it (Matthew 28:19), and it is the God-given sign of what he has done for you: in it you publicly confess your faith and picture your washing from sin, your death and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:3–4), and your entry into his visible church. It does not make you a Christian, but a Christian who refuses it disobeys his Lord. It is not a reward for maturity but the first step of obedience: if you have trusted Christ and not been baptised as a believer, speak to your pastor.

How do I know I have been born again? Not by remembering the moment, which many believers cannot, but by its fruit: faith in Christ, love for God and his people, a new attitude to sin, a desire for his word, a life that is changing, however slowly (1 John 3:9–10, 14; 5:1). You did not cause it, but you can see that you are alive. If you trust Christ, you have been born again, because no one comes to Christ unless the Spirit has given him life. If you are unsure, do not stare inward; look to Christ and ask him for life. He gives the Spirit to those who ask.

Where Christians differ: does baptism regenerate? Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some Anglican traditions take the washing of regeneration to mean baptism, which in their view causes or conveys the new birth, and they point also to John 3:5 and 1 Peter 3:21. This commentary’s view: The washing is the Spirit’s inner cleansing, which baptism pictures but does not cause. Paul has just said salvation is not by works done by us; a ritual performed by us that caused regeneration would contradict it. The new birth is the Spirit’s sovereign work, like the wind (John 3:8), received by faith (Galatians 3:26–27). Jesus spoke to Nicodemus before Christian baptism existed, in the language of Ezekiel’s cleansing water, and Peter at once explains that he means not the removal of dirt but an appeal to God for a good conscience. Scripture shows people regenerated before baptism (Acts 10:44–48) and baptised without being regenerated (Acts 8:13, 20–23). Baptism is the outward sign of the inward washing, rightly given to those who profess faith (Acts 2:38, 41). Reformed Christians who baptise the children of believers agree that the water does not itself regenerate, and this commentary gladly counts them faithful brothers.

Uncertain wording. The compressed Greek can be read two ways: one washing that is both regeneration and renewal, the Spirit cleansing away sin’s defilement and creating new life (most likely), or two things side by side, the washing of regeneration and the Spirit’s renewal. Either way the whole work is the Spirit’s.

verseByVerse.quote: whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God poured out his Spirit lavishly on us through Christ, so that, declared righteous by grace, we are now heirs of eternal life.

Whom he poured out on us richly. The language of Pentecost (Acts 2:17), now happening to a scatter of Cretan believers. Richly means lavishly: not rationed by merit or maturity, but poured on the people who were hating one another in verse 3.

Through Jesus Christ our Saviour. Peter explained Pentecost the same way: being exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you see and hear (Acts 2:33). The pouring on Crete is the gift of a risen and enthroned Saviour.

The whole Trinity. All three persons are at work in one sentence: the Father’s kindness (v. 4), the Spirit’s renewal (v. 5), through Christ the Saviour (v. 6). Paul cannot describe salvation without all three.

Justified by his grace. The courtroom word: God the Judge declares sinners righteous in his sight, freely, not because they are righteous in themselves (Romans 4:5). Justification is distinct from regeneration (God’s work in us) but always accompanies it.

We might become heirs. Justified sinners are adopted as God’s children and heirs (Galatians 4:7). An acquitted man walks out of court owing nothing and owning nothing; Paul says we walk out as heirs. The court declares us not guilty, and the Father writes us into the will.

According to the hope of eternal life. The hope of the letter’s first sentence (1:2), promised by the God who never lies: the letter has come round to where it started.

Not pardoned only, but brought in. The Father did not merely pardon us and send us away; he brought us in. God appointed the Son the heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and those joined to him are fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17), so the inheritance is Christ’s own, shared with us. His kindness planned it, the Son’s blood and righteousness secured it, and the Spirit, poured out without stint on people who had hated one another, seals it in their hearts; and the God who never lies has promised it.

Why does it matter whether justification is a declaration or a process? Because it decides where your assurance rests. If you are made righteous over time, you can never be sure you are righteous enough. If you are justified by God’s declaration on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, your standing is as secure as Christ’s, complete from the moment you believe; it cannot be improved or lost. Sanctification is real and necessary, but you pursue it as a child already accepted, not as a defendant awaiting the verdict.

What does it mean that the Spirit was poured out richly on me, when I feel so dry? That he has been given to you in fullness, whatever you feel. Every believer has the Spirit (Romans 8:9); there is no second class of Christians with less of him. Dry seasons come to the godliest, as the psalms show, but the Spirit is still keeping you in faith, convicting you of sin, drawing you to Christ. Seek to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18) by the means he uses: the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and fellowship. Ask God for a fresh sense of his presence, and he will not give you a stone.

Where Christians differ: is justification a declaration, or a process of becoming righteous? Roman Catholic teaching holds that justification includes the infusion of righteousness, so that a person is made righteous over time and may grow in justification. This commentary’s view: Justification is a once-for-all legal declaration by God that the believing sinner is righteous in his sight, on the basis of Christ’s righteousness imputed to him, received by faith alone. Our sins are counted to Christ, and his righteousness is counted to us (double imputation, 2 Corinthians 5:21). Sanctification, the process of being made holy, follows and is inseparable, but it is not the ground of our acceptance.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are excellent and profitable for people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This gospel of free grace is utterly reliable, and Titus must press it home, because it is what makes believers eager to do good.

The saying is trustworthy. One of five trustworthy sayings in Paul’s letters to Timothy and Titus (the others are 1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11). It points back to verses 4–7, perhaps an early creed or hymn.

Insist on these things. Affirm them strongly and keep affirming them (diabebaiousthai), the word used of the false teachers’ confident assertions (1 Timothy 1:7): Titus is to press this doctrine as confidently.

So that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. The logic runs the opposite way from what we expect. Having excluded works from salvation as thoroughly as language allows, Paul says: insist on that, so that people will do good works. Free grace is not balanced by a warning about effort; it drives the effort, and the Spirit poured out richly (v. 6) is its power. “Be careful” means to give the mind to it: good works are planned, not left to chance. “Devote themselves” means to take the lead in them: Christians are to be in the business of good works.

These things are excellent and profitable for people. For believers and the wider society alike, unlike the unprofitable controversies of the next verse.

Created in Christ Jesus for this. How can the same gospel exclude works so completely and then produce them so reliably? Because it joins people to Christ: we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:10). The more clearly a believer sees that Christ has done everything for him, the more freely Christ works through him.

He commends what he supplied. The God who saved us by mercy alone supplies the good works he then rewards: he planned them, gives the will and strength to do them, and on the last day will say well done. He takes former slaves of appetite and haters of one another, sets them to work for the good of a whole island, and then, astonishingly, commends them for it.

What it does not mean. Not that good works earn salvation. They are the fruit and evidence of saving faith (Ephesians 2:10; James 2:17–18). Even the best are flawed, and they are accepted because Christ obeyed perfectly in our place and his righteousness is counted as ours (Romans 5:19; Philippians 3:9).

In everyday life. The meal for a new mother arrives because someone noticed and put it on the calendar: that is Paul’s “careful”, grace that thinks ahead. What could you take the lead in, without waiting to be asked?

If I am saved by grace alone, why should I work so hard at good works? Because grace has made you a child of God, and children love to please their Father. Because Christ gave himself to make you zealous for good works (2:14), and to neglect them is to neglect what he died for. Because they glorify God, draw others to him (Matthew 5:16) and bless people in need. And because they are the evidence that your faith is real. You do not work for your salvation; you work from it, with the energy of someone who has nothing to prove and everything to give.

Uncertain wording. “Devote themselves” (proistēmi, again in v. 14) usually means to stand at the head of something, and so give oneself to it; but it was also used of practising a trade, so it could mean to engage in honourable occupations, as some translations note in the margin. Devotion to good works fits the letter’s refrain best (2:7, 14; 3:1), though honest work would suit an island known for “lazy gluttons” (1:12), and a believer’s daily work is one of his good works.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church saved by grace spends itself on people, not on arguments. Paul tells Titus to shun worthless quarrels about genealogies and the law (v. 9) and, after two warnings, to refuse a man who keeps dividing the church (vv. 10–11). Then the travel plans turn into a last lesson: send Zenas and Apollos on their way with everything they need, and let the believers learn to meet urgent needs and not be unfruitful (vv. 12–14). The letter ends, as it began, with grace (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Divisive Man, and the Limit on Patience

The divisive man (hairetikos) is warned twice, and then left (v.10). Paul requires patience, and sets a limit to it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Controversies are ‘unprofitable’ (v.9), set against good works that are ‘profitable’ (v.8).

Now: The letter's refrain lands on something small: see that two travellers lack nothing (vv.13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless. As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him, knowing that such a person is warped and sinful; he is self-condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not spend the church’s strength on pointless arguments, and do not let one man go on dividing it: warn him twice, then have nothing more to do with him.

Avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law. Shun them; do not try to win them (2 Timothy 2:16, 23). The genealogies were probably speculations built on Old Testament family trees (see Uncertain wording below), the same trouble as at Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:4); the quarrels were the circumcision party’s fights over the law of Moses (1:10, 14).

Unprofitable and worthless. The language of profit and loss, set against the “profitable” of verse 8: every hour spent on quarrels about the law is an hour not spent on cases of urgent need (v. 14).

The law’s quarrels ended at the cross. Why are quarrels about God’s own law worthless? Because Christ has fulfilled it. By his death he broke down the dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile, abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances (Ephesians 2:14–15). The circumcision party on Crete were fighting over a wall Christ had already demolished. To reopen them as though they decided who belongs to God was not zeal for Scripture but refusal of what the cross had settled.

A person who stirs up division. Verses 10–11 finish what chapter 1 began: the empty talkers had to be silenced (1:10–11), and here is what to do with a man who will not be. The word (hairetikos) gives us heretic, but then meant someone who forms parties around his own opinions and splits the church. The offence is not chiefly wrong belief but the splitting of a congregation.

After warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him. Patience and due process: two warnings give a chance to repent (Matthew 18:15–17), and a church that removes someone without clear warnings has not followed this text. But there is no third warning: endless patience with a man who is dividing a church is not kindness to the church.

Warped and sinful; he is self-condemned. “Warped” is literally turned inside out. Told twice, plainly, and persisting, he has convicted himself out of his own mouth; Titus is not the one who condemns him.

The church he is building. The church holds together not because its members win their arguments but because its Lord holds it. He prayed that his people would be one, then gave his own body to make them one body. He is patient with the quarrelsome, warning before he judges and running to meet every wanderer who turns back. And he guards what he has bought: neither a divisive man in Crete nor the gates of hell will prevail against the church he is building.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone who disagrees with church leaders should be excluded. The issue is a divisive spirit that splits the church over foolish matters and refuses correction. If you are a tender-hearted believer who worries that you have been divisive, your very willingness to be corrected sets you apart from the man Paul describes, who has been warned twice and will not hear.

How do I tell a foolish controversy from a necessary one? Ask whether Scripture speaks clearly to it and whether it touches the gospel or godliness. Titus must rebuke false teachers sharply (1:13) and refute those who contradict sound doctrine (1:9), so defending the truth is not optional. Paul forbids arguments built on speculation or on things Scripture does not settle, debates pursued for the pleasure of winning, and quarrels that feed curiosity and pride rather than faith and love. Test: is this debate making anyone more like Christ, or only more certain they are right?

What does “have nothing more to do with him” mean in practice? After two warnings the church is to put him out of its fellowship (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5:11–13). He should not teach, lead or keep spreading division, and believers should stop debating with him or giving him an audience. But the aim is still repentance: do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Be courteous, pray for him, and welcome him back gladly if he repents.

Uncertain wording. What these genealogies were is not known for certain. Most think of legend spun out of the Old Testament family lists, as in Jewish retellings of Genesis from this period; some, of pedigrees used to claim spiritual privilege. Either way they went with the “Jewish myths” of 1:14 and fed argument, not godliness.

verseByVerse.quote: When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. Do your best to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way; see that they lack nothing. And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul arranges for Titus to be relieved and asks the churches to equip two travelling teachers, and he makes even that errand a lesson in good works.

Artemas or Tychicus. Artemas appears nowhere else in Scripture; Tychicus carried Ephesians and Colossians (Ephesians 6:21). One of them will replace Titus in Crete: Paul does not pull a man out of a post without putting someone in it.

Nicopolis. The name means city of victory. Probably it is the one on the west coast of Greece, founded by Augustus after his victory at Actium (see Uncertain wording below), a good base for winter and for mission into Dalmatia, where Titus later went (2 Timothy 4:10). A season’s work planned suggests Paul was free, between his first Roman imprisonment and the final one, from which he wrote 2 Timothy (see the introduction).

Zenas the lawyer and Apollos. Zenas is otherwise unknown. Apollos was the eloquent teacher from Alexandria, mighty in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24–28). They were probably carrying this letter. To speed them on their way is the regular term for supplying missionaries with food, money and travel needs (Romans 15:24; 3 John 6).

See that they lack nothing. Travelling teachers depended on the churches, and Paul is specific about it in a letter he could have ended three verses earlier. The Lord himself came as a traveller with nowhere to lay his head, dependent on others’ hospitality, and he counts every cup of water given to his servants as given to him.

Let our people learn. Verse 14 turns the errand into a lesson. Good works do not come naturally; the Spirit grows them as believers learn, practise and cultivate them, and “devote themselves” is the word of verse 8.

So as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful. Not general benevolence but the emergency in front of you, such as Zenas and Apollos passing through. Cretans known as “lazy gluttons” (1:12) must become known for working and giving. Unfruitful is a farming word: a tree that produces nothing is a failure at being a tree (Matthew 7:17–20). So the letter’s great refrain lands on something small and concrete: make sure two travellers have what they need. That is what devotion to good works looked like on Crete that week.

Fruit from the vine. Paul’s farming word echoes Jesus: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). The Cretans are to learn as branches learn: staying joined to Christ, drawing on his life, and letting it come out in practical help wherever the need is urgent.

What it does not mean. Not that fruitfulness is measured only by visible results. It is the overflow of a life devoted to Christ, often growing slowly and out of sight. A believer who fears he is barren but still clings to Christ is a branch in the vine, and the one who began a good work in him will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

How do I learn to devote myself to good works? As you learn any skill: by practice, example and planning. Copy believers who are good at it. Ask where the urgent needs are this week: the neighbour after surgery, the family short of money, the student far from home. Set aside money and time in advance, and start with what is in front of you rather than waiting for a grand opportunity. And do it as worship: whatever you do for the least of Christ’s brothers you do for him (Matthew 25:40).

How should my church care for missionaries and visiting preachers? Generously and thoughtfully, so that they lack nothing. Pay their expenses and give a proper gift, not a token; offer a bed, meals, a quiet place to rest; ask what they actually need. Pray for them specifically, and support missionaries over the long term, not only when they visit. We ought to support people like these, says John, that we may be fellow workers for the truth (3 John 8). A church that sends its gospel workers on their way well shares in their reward.

Uncertain wording. “Lawyer” (nomikos) could mean an expert in the law of Moses, as usually in the Gospels, or a Roman jurist; nothing else is known of Zenas. And several cities were called Nicopolis; the one on the west coast of Greece is likeliest, being large and well placed, but Paul does not say.
verseByVerse.note: Nicopolis was probably the city of that name on the west coast of Greece. Apollos was the gifted teacher from Alexandria.

verseByVerse.quote: All who are with me send greetings to you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul closes with greetings to those who love him in the faith, and a last wish of grace for the whole church.

Those who love us in the faith. Unusually, Paul names none of the companions sending greetings. The letter has been full of people who did not love him; at the end he sends his greeting past them to the ones who do, and “in the faith” shows what binds them: not mere personal affection, but the love of people who believe the same gospel.

With you all. “You all” is plural: the letter was addressed to one man but read aloud to the congregations, so the last word goes to everyone listening: the elders being appointed, the older women told not to slander, the young wives, the slaves not pilfering, and even, one supposes, the divisive man who still had two warnings coming.

The first word and the last. A letter full of instructions about good works ends, as it began (1:4), with grace. Grace is the letter’s argument, and in this letter it always has a face. It appeared in Jesus Christ; it was paid for when he gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness (2:14); it reaches us through the Spirit poured out through him (3:6). To wish a church grace is to wish it Christ: his favour, his presence and his power with every one of them.

It was enough for Crete. To an island proverbial for lying, gluttony and disorder, God sent a short letter about decent elders, ordinary duties and grace, and it was enough, because the grace was his, the God who never lies. That grace has never run short. It was enough for Crete, and it is with all his people still.

Why does Paul end every letter with grace? Because grace is not only how the Christian life begins but how it continues and ends. We are saved, trained and kept by grace, and will be brought home by grace. Every instruction in this letter assumes it, and none can be obeyed without it. Grace be with you all is not a pleasant sign-off; it names the one thing that makes everything else possible, and hands them back to the God who supplies it.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work,<sup>2</sup>to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people.<sup>3</sup>For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another.<sup>4</sup>But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared,<sup>5</sup>he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit,<sup>6</sup>whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior,<sup>7</sup>so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.<sup>8</sup>The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are excellent and profitable for people.<sup>9</sup>But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless.<sup>10</sup>As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him,<sup>11</sup>knowing that such a person is warped and sinful; he is self-condemned.<sup>12</sup>When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there.<sup>13</sup>Do your best to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way; see that they lack nothing.<sup>14</sup>And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful.<sup>15</sup>All who are with me send greetings to you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.

keyVerse.quote: he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this verse. The gentleness asked in verses 1–2 rests on it, the bleak memory of verse 3 is answered by it, and the good works of verse 8 flow from it. It shuts out even our best works as the reason we are saved and puts the whole cause in God’s mercy, so the people it saves have nothing to boast of and every reason to be kind.

3.reflection:
Paul grounds courtesy toward everyone in the memory of what we once were (vv. 2–3). Who do you find it hardest to be gentle with, in public life or close to home, and how does verse 3 change the way you see them?

Verse 5 excludes even “works done by us in righteousness” from the reason God saved us. Why is that harder for respectable people to accept than for those with an obvious past, and what does it leave room for?

Titus must insist on free grace so that believers devote themselves to good works (v. 8). How does grace produce good works rather than excuse us from them? What good work could you plan for, instead of leaving it to chance?

Verses 9–14 set worthless quarrels against meeting urgent needs. Where are you tempted to spend your energy on arguments, and what urgent need around you, like two travellers needing supplies, is waiting for someone to take the lead?
